analysis.one_liner: Lets the government sue tobacco companies in one class action to recover Medicare and Medicaid costs of smoking-related illness.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote, and taxpayers kept paying the Medicare and Medicaid bills for tobacco-related illness.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have authorized the Attorney General to sue cigarette makers in a single federal class action to recover what Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans' health programs have paid to treat diseases caused by smoking. It cited billions in annual costs to those programs and let the government prove its case with statistics rather than individual patient records. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and the Medicare and Medicaid programs would gain: money now spent treating tobacco-related disease would be recovered from the manufacturers who sold the products, easing pressure on the Medicare trust funds the bill says were projected toward insolvency.

how_it_helps.text: It authorizes the Attorney General to sue tobacco manufacturers in one class action to recover Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans' health payments for tobacco-caused illness, without having to identify each individual beneficiary [S2].

The bill's findings cite roughly $16 billion a year in Medicare inpatient costs and $3 billion in Medicaid inpatient costs for tobacco-related illness in fiscal 1994, and estimate at least $800 billion in costs to Medicare trust funds over 20 years [S3].
Money recovered would go back to the programs that paid: states get their Medicaid share, Medicare trust funds get repaid, and the rest goes to the Treasury [S3].
It lets the government use statistical and epidemiological evidence and market-share liability to prove causation and damages, easing the proof burden that normally makes such suits hard to win [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco product manufacturers, who could be held liable — under market-share and industry-wide theories — for billions in federal health payments for smoking-related disease.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly relaxed the government's burden: causation and damages could be proven by statistical or epidemiological evidence, and liability could be imposed on market-share or industry-wide theories rather than on proof that a specific company caused a specific patient's illness [S3].

Tobacco manufacturers would face potentially enormous judgments for decades of Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans' care, a cost that could be passed on to consumers through higher cigarette prices and could threaten companies' viability [S3].
Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries would have had no notice of the suit and no right to join it, so any individual claims they might have would proceed separately [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would have shifted enormous tobacco-related health costs from taxpayers to an industry whose own documents, per the bill's findings, showed it knew nicotine was addictive and concealed that information [S3]. Drawbacks: it was drafted to make the government's case as easy as possible (statistical causation, market-share liability, no class notice), which critics would call a tilted suit, and a large judgment would likely have been passed to consumers through higher cigarette prices. Since it died in committee, its real-world cost was zero; its real-world effect was that taxpayers kept paying those costs.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late June 1994 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, it sat there and never got a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg introduced S. 2245 on June 28, 1994, with Senator Tom Harkin as cosponsor [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 with the bill still in committee, so it never reached the Senate floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, who avoided a potentially massive federal suit to recoup health care costs, while taxpayers kept paying those bills.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 28, 1994 and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both named sponsors were Democrats, and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of the never-held floor fight cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to a federal class action to recoup billions in government health payments for tobacco-caused disease, using relaxed proof rules and market-share liability. It died in committee, so they never faced it.

industries.industry: Medicare and Medicaid programs and their beneficiaries
industries.note: Recovered funds would repay Medicare trust funds and state Medicaid agencies, shoring up programs facing the insolvency the bill cites. Taxpayers would shoulder less of the cost of tobacco-related illness.
